summary: Defined an IPv6 aggregatable global unicast address format, designed to let addresses be grouped for efficient routing. It is now historic and was replaced by RFC 3587.

eli5.summary: An old plan for how long internet addresses should be split up so routers can handle them more easily. It has since been replaced.

questions: ipv6 aggregatable global unicast address format
how is an ipv6 address structured
what is address aggregation in ipv6
how many subnets does ipv6 support per site
subtitle: A hierarchical structure for IPv6 addresses to enable scalable routing

tldr.problem: IPv6 needs a way to structure addresses so routers can efficiently aggregate them and build smaller routing tables.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines a hierarchical format dividing IPv6 addresses into layers: top-level aggregation (TLA) for major providers, next-level aggregation (NLA) for organizations, site-level aggregation (SLA) for subnets, and interface identifiers.
tldr.outcome: This format became historic when RFC 3587 redefined IPv6 address aggregation with different field sizes and scoping.

today: RFC 2374 is Historic and has been superseded by RFC 3587, which redefines the IPv6 aggregatable global unicast address format with revised field allocations and updated terminology to reflect modern Internet structure.

sections.title: Introduction and Overview
sections.content:
RFC 2374 defines the structure of aggregatable global unicast addresses for IPv6, the Internet's next-generation protocol. IPv6 addresses are 128 bits long, and rather than leave that space unstructured, this RFC divides it into hierarchical layers that help routers forward traffic efficiently.

The key insight is that routers do not need to know the structure inside an IPv6 address to forward it, but address structure helps Internet service providers and network operators assign blocks of addresses in a way that scales the routing system. By grouping addresses hierarchically, a router can forward based on the first few bits and does not need to store individual routes for every single address.
sections.eli5: Think of postal addresses: the router is like a mail truck that only needs to know which country first, then which city, then which neighborhood. It does not need to memorize every house address.

sections.title: The Address Structure
sections.content:
The address format divides a 128-bit IPv6 address into six parts:

Format Prefix (FP): 3 bits identifying this as an aggregatable global unicast address (always 001 in binary).

Top-Level Aggregation (TLA) ID: 13 bits designating a top-level provider or Internet backbone organization. This yields 8,192 possible TLA identifiers.

Reserved: 8 bits set aside for future growth of the TLA or NLA fields.

Next-Level Aggregation (NLA) ID: 24 bits allowing organizations assigned a TLA ID to create their own addressing hierarchy and identify customer sites.

Site-Level Aggregation (SLA) ID: 16 bits for a single organization to divide its address space into subnets, supporting up to 65,535 subnets.

Interface ID: 64 bits to uniquely identify a device on a link, typically based on its hardware address in IEEE EUI-64 format.
sections.eli5: The address is divided like a postal code: the first part identifies the global region, the next identifies the company managing that region, the next identifies a customer organization, the next identifies a subnet inside that organization, and the last identifies a device on that subnet.

sections.title: How Routing Aggregation Works
sections.content:
Routers at the Internet core need to know about every active TLA ID so they can forward packets to the right top-level providers. The RFC recommends keeping this number close to 8,192 entries to remain within the scaling limits of routing hardware available in 1998.

Within a TLA, routers can use the NLA ID to aggregate further, and within a site, the SLA ID creates a fourth level of hierarchy. This multi-level structure allows efficient routing: a router in North America does not need to know the detailed topology of Europe; it only needs to know which TLA handles European addresses.

The choice of 13 bits for TLA was a careful engineering trade-off. Fewer bits would not provide enough top-level identifiers; more bits would exceed what routing technology could handle while maintaining stability.
sections.eli5: A mail truck in New York only needs to know which big post office zone Europe belongs to, not the details of every European neighborhood. Routers work the same way: they aggregate addresses into larger and larger regions.

sections.title: Flexibility and Extensibility
sections.content:
The 8-bit Reserved field allows the TLA and NLA fields to grow in the future if routing technology improves. If routers eventually can handle more top-level entries, the Reserved bits can be allocated to TLA, increasing the maximum to roughly 2 million TLA identifiers.

Organizations assigned a TLA ID may build hierarchies within their NLA space, allowing them to support other organizations in turn. A provider might use some of the NLA space for their own sites and delegate other parts to regional networks, who may in turn delegate further.

At the site level, an organization has full control of how it structures the SLA field. Some organizations may use it flat (assigning independent subnet identifiers with no hierarchy), while others may create a two-level hierarchy by splitting the 16 bits between a region code and a subnet code.
sections.eli5: The design leaves room to grow if needed, and every organization can split up its assigned space in whatever way makes sense for its own network.

sections.title: Interface Identifiers and Hardware Addresses
sections.content:
Interface identifiers are 64 bits and must be unique on the link they inhabit. Where possible, they are derived from hardware media access control (MAC) addresses. The RFC specifies that they must be constructed in IEEE EUI-64 format, a 64-bit extension of IEEE 48-bit MAC addresses.

A particular bit called the universal/local (u) bit marks whether the identifier is globally unique or only locally unique. If a device has a globally unique MAC address, the u bit is set to indicate global scope; if the identifier was generated locally (for example, on a point-to-point link), the u bit indicates that.

The procedures for creating EUI-64 identifiers from hardware addresses are defined in the IPv6 addressing architecture specification and in link-specific RFCs such as those describing IPv6 over Ethernet or IPv6 over FDDI.
sections.eli5: The last 64 bits of the address identify a single device, usually derived from its physical hardware address so that each device has a unique identity on its local network.
